items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: Elephants need hairs to STAY COOL
items.claim: Big animals are well-insulated by sheer size — surface area to volume ratio drops as you scale up. So why do elephants have sparse but persistent hairs, in a hot environment where insulation is the last thing they need?
items.prompt: What's the function of an elephant's hairs?

options.text: They INCREASE convective heat loss — the sparse hairs disrupt the still air layer at the skin surface and allow more efficient cooling than bare skin would

items.reveal_title: Surface area scaling and thermal management
items.reveal:
Animal mass scales as length cubed; surface area as length squared. Doubling an animal's linear size doubles its surface-to-volume ratio's inverse — large animals have proportionally less surface area to dump heat through.

Elephants generate huge metabolic heat (about 2500 watts at rest for a 4 tonne adult) but have proportionally tiny skin. They are constantly battling overheating. Their hairs, ears (huge for their body), wallowing in mud, and behavioural cooling all serve heat dissipation.

Cordeschi and colleagues (2012) modelled elephant hair density and showed sparse hairs improve heat loss by about 5 to 20 percent — likely a real evolutionary purpose.
items.why: Hair is associated with warmth. For animals at the wrong end of the surface-to-volume scaling, hair can do the opposite.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.
